candidates.text:
I am getting lots of incoming questions about the public execution of Nidal Hasan, mostly because I have been outspoken on wanting public executions for over a decade.

My position is simple:  Executions should be public and brutal, not private and medicalized.  They are the ultimate example of the state's monopoly on violence, and the only way to keep that from running out of control is to confront voters with the trade they have made every single time, that they might have appropiate confidence or revulsion in the institution.

This is not new thinking.  George Washington thought the same.  The way we have shifted from hanging to firing squads to doctors quietly injecting chemicals that send our worst gently off to sleep is awful and dystopian, a total short-circuiting of important feedback mechanisms.  It makes needless executions more likely, not less so.  People who demean this as barbaric or yucky miss the whole point.  It doesn't somehow become torture or inhumane (as the UN is suddenly claiming) just because we decline to hide the act behind a curtain.

And then there are those who suggest any revel in the death of those who truly deserve it is an indicator of a broken or diseased mind.  To the contrary.  It is normal, good, and aligned with our natural and national order.  That it has not been done here in 60 years is an indictment in and of itself.

And that is without even getting into the fact that men were not hung for stealing horse, but that horses may not be stolen.

"I would to God that one of the most attrocious in each State was hung in Gibbets, up on a gallows five times as high as the one prepared by Haman. No punishment, in my opinion, is too great for the Man, who can build his greatness upon his Country’s ruin." 
- George Washington, 1778

candidates.text:
Before you spend another dollar on ads, run your welcome emails through this prompt.

Every subscriber your ads bring in gets these emails first.

Paste this into ChatGPT or Claude, then add your popup and your emails at the bottom:

"Audit my ecommerce welcome email series. Below I'll paste my signup popup (the offer and any question it asks), whether the series stops when someone buys, and every welcome email in order with its subject line, preview text, send delay, buttons, and body copy. If you can, also attach a phone screenshot of each email.

Check it against these rules:

1. Email 1 sends right after signup, with no delay.
2. The promised code or offer is in the first lines of email 1, before any brand story.
3. The series has 5 to 7 emails spread over 10 to 14 days.
4. Across the series, it covers why the brand started, the problem the product solves, how it solves it, one specific customer review, and the biggest reason people hesitate (price, fit, quality, or shipping).
5. Each email asks for one action. Several buttons are fine if they all go to the same place.
6. If my popup asks a question, later emails use the answer. If it doesn't, an early email asks what they're shopping for.
7. If the offer expires, the last email gives the exact date and time.
8. The series stops once someone buys.
9. Each subject line makes clear what's inside, and the preview text adds to it instead of repeating it or showing filler like "View in browser."
10. If I attached screenshots, check each email on mobile: the offer and main button show without scrolling, the text is easy to read, and it doesn't rely on one big image.

Then give me:

1. Every fix, ranked by how much it likely affects sales. For each one, quote the line from my email that has the problem, say why it matters in one sentence, and give the fix.
2. Rewrites I can paste for the top 3 fixes, in my brand's voice. Don't make up reviews, numbers, or facts about my brand. Use [brackets] for anything I need to fill in.
3. Any rule you couldn't check from what I pasted.

My popup: [paste]
Does the series stop when someone buys? [yes / no / not sure]
My emails: [paste]"

It checks your series against the welcome series rules I teach, then ranks the fixes and rewrites the top 3.

The backstory here is funny… 

This guy built an $8 million music business where the musicians were fake, the fans were fake, and the money was real.

He did 10x the number of streams as Taylor Swift during the scheme 😂

Michael Smith used up to 10,000 bot accounts to stream songs he controlled and collect the royalties.

But playing the same few songs millions of times would look suspicious. He needed, in his words, “a TON of songs fast.”

So he used AI to generate hundreds of thousands of tracks. Spread the fake listeners across enough fake music and each song attracts less attention.

By April 2023, the numbers were absurd.

Taylor Swift’s entire catalog: 9.3 million streams.

Smith’s AI songs: 80.9 million. 😂😂

Same month. Same service. Both counting YouTube Music family-plan streams.

His broader scheme ran from 2017 to 2024, diverting royalty money from actual artists.

He just got 18 months in prison and an order to forfeit $8.09 million.

And because Trump recently ordered federal agencies to replace “Artificial Intelligence” with “Super Intelligence,” the DOJ’s actual headline calls this “Super Intelligence-Assisted Music Streaming Fraud.”

The man automated the music, the audience, and the revenue.

Unfortunately, he got a little carried away 😂

Do We Need Steve Wozniak?

It's not clear you need technical co-founders anymore for most startups.

The tech is not the moat.

Still need a strong core : a solutions architect (maybe).

But, the marginal hire is as close to the customer as possible.

In fact, we’re now hiring product managers over engineers.

A smart PM can run 3x faster than engineers since they have clear vision and customer feedback.

*The distance between the customer and the CEO is shrinking*

If you play it out, the feedback a CEO might give to a PM could simply flow directly to an AI.

So, why not let the CEO run the AI?

1) Latency & opportunity cost of time
3) Need for iteration with customers 
4) Domain expertise ('context')

In the fullness of time, even the PM role may not be necessary.

What you would need then is someone who can think commercially: GTM owners.

What is the end-state - when latency and cost is low, and speed of feedback is high?

It seems to resemble a real time strategy like World of Warcraft or Ender’s Game.

In ten years, the CEO is wired up to agents via neuralink in something that resembles a real-time strategy game.

If you listen to how Jensen manages dozens of direct reports on emails we aren't too off from that.

And, if you look at what Huberman is saying about the ambitions of $META and other firms - they are already thinking about this end-state where the gap between the customer and the creator is as narrow as possible.

candidates.text:
Many acquisition processes fall into this category.

A founder recently said he changed the company's direction and got board approval to sell after a strategic acquirer made a 9-figure offer, including a lot of cash upfront.

Investors would've made a return, and founders would've made life changing money.

7-8 months into the process, the CEO changed.

The new CEO decided the deal was too small for the company and killed it.

This startup was now out of runway and, unfortunately, also lost revenue during the process.

They couldn't turn the ship around (grow again), so they ran a sale process. Nothing came from it.

Eventually, someone else acquihired the team, but the product and the company are likely going to die.

It's unfortunate, but it happens more often than expected.

Most founders think it'll be different for them. They throw caution to the wind.

candidates.text:
I think travel is so important because I believe that consciously shaping and building the life you want is the highest-leverage activity you can do as a young person. 

Traveling and seeing other people allows you to see what kind of people they can shape up to be and you can have a very clear view of what you don't want to be versus what you do want to be.

I was in a club in Pokhara, Nepal, a few days ago and I saw these two uncles, fat and balding, drunk on alcohol in a club, just on phones, recording themselves while having a glass in their hand.

And no shade to them. I don't think that there's anything wrong with that. To be honest it's great that they were enjoying it. It's just that I would not want to be that person when I grow up.

I would not want to be the type of person that is half drunk, not physically fit, slightly balding, in a club, alone (sort of alone with no friends), weirdly taking videos of myself dancing weirdly as if I was a 15-year-old using Snapchat 

And that made me realize that I should be doing everything in my power to consciously build a life that that leads to me being in that state at the age of 55 

I believe a lot of us are playing and losing at the game we wouldn't want to win either way.

Which means understanding which games to play, which outcomes you wish for, and which outcomes you don't care about even if you end up winning is super, super important .

So the solution remains to go out there and look at the 50- to 60-year-olds whose life you genuinely find interesting and you would genuinely want to emulate that when you reach that age (even if it is being semi-drunk in a club in Nepal, dancing alone and recording yourself, or something else). Then actively take actions so that your life leads to that person.

The problem arises when you consider it automatic or not in your hands. When it truly, truly is in your hands: the type of person you become or the type of life you build, even with the current constraints and problems you have
